title: fix: prevent Code Mode worker OOM after databases close
body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes Code Mode workers running out of memory after a long-running Gateway has opened and closed many databases. Closed SQLite admissions retained full schema and row-write metadata, which every new worker inherited.

## User Impact

Workers can start after hundreds of databases close, using the existing memory limits. Open siblings continue sharing validation facts; reopening after the final connection closes validates again. No migration or operator action is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The admission registry retires payloads after the final native connection closes or its worker exits. Only the host decides final retirement, because a worker can have an older view of its siblings. Reopening creates a fresh admission; both scoped and unscoped row-cache tokens identify that generation.

The existing open-identity map guards repeated close callbacks. Intermediate handle count changes use the shared cells directly; only a thread's first/final handle publishes and exchanges metadata. Minimal host-owned identity descriptors remain until explicit retirement to preserve SQLite POSIX locks.

Production is +199/-159 lines (net +40), down from net +122 in the first revision. The reduction removes the parallel close-tracking WeakSet and duplicate connection ownership, consolidates generation reads/increments and schema revocation, and unifies the committed/pending scoped-token construction. Tests are +451/-65 lines.

## Evidence

- The original owner retained 300 closed records: 41,504,700 serialized bytes. The real Code Mode worker failed with `ERR_WORKER_OUT_OF_MEMORY`. The final reproducer retains zero records (2 serialized bytes); the same worker starts after 300 closes with 21,287,536 bytes of heap, under its unchanged 64 MiB limit.
- The owner regression passes all 6 tests in 19.99 seconds wall time (17.70 seconds in Vitest, dominated by shared compiler preparation). It covers final close, reopen, failed initial admission, stale snapshots, 300 closed databases, explicit descriptor retirement, and direct/retained workers. A two-worker negative control reproduced premature retirement before the host-only fix; both variants now preserve the later sibling. A real SQLite negative control also reproduced an unscoped-token collision across close/reopen and different committed updates; generation-aware committed/pending tokens now pass that regression. Admission, format, and worker tests pass.
- The final cross-lane run passes 1,197 tests across 82 files in 795.77 seconds wall time. The 83-file inventory retains only the existing PostgreSQL transaction-lock service-dependent skip. Existing platform-specific skips remain. Admission, format, corruption, ownership, session, and worker tests are covered.
- Validation: the full `node scripts/check-changed.mjs --base 27be5cd3a50a3674b2d31e4ebf6912d7c9d29b09 --timed` run exits 0 in 773.90 seconds, including all core/test typechecks, dead-export scans, lint, and production guards; the final Madge run exits 0 with zero cycles. Independent Codex review of the final staged candidate is clean through P2. All proof used local synthetic data and isolated state; no remote leases or live Gateway state were used.
- Performance gate is still blocked: the shared host remained only 40–59% idle after this lane's validation stopped, with other CI compiler work active. No other lane's process was stopped, and no idle comparison is claimed. The final broad run's deletion cases passed (active 45.705s, restart-draining 41.804s, legacy-retiring 32.270s); the earlier baseline restart-draining result was 49.888s. Those are unmatched runs and do not establish a speedup or regression. The required same-command, back-to-back idle baseline/candidate comparison remains outstanding before landing. No timeout, retry, or assertion was relaxed.
